To address this challenge, we developed an innovative method to monitor soil activity in situ by imaging.

title: Observing soil organisms in situ?
text: Soil is a major reservoir of biodiversity, hosting more than a quarter of all terrestrial biodiversity. Yet its opacity and the cryptic nature of the organisms living in it make it an especially difficult environment to study. title: Observing soil organisms in situ?
text:
The device
The system relies on desktop flatbed scanners, adapted to field conditions and buried in the soil. In the field, each scanner is paired with an automated control module based on a Raspberry Pi, which handles image acquisition. This setup allows long-term, high-resolution acquisition campaigns with minimal human intervention.






Schematic of the buried scanner device







Automated control module based on a Raspberry Pi







6 h between two images


1200 dpi image resolution


A4 scanned surface


> 1 mm size of monitored organisms

title: Observing soil organisms in situ?
text:
What the images reveal
Images are acquired every six hours at 1200 dpi over an A4 surface. This makes it possible to monitor the activity of organisms larger than one millimetre, including root structures, some fungal structures and many invertebrate taxa. It also allows their dynamics to be followed at a fine temporal scale and over long periods.


Roots and fungi

Colonization of oak roots by ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungi observed by in situ imaging.


Invertebrates

Mutualism between aphids and ants on roots observed by in situ imaging.


Roots and fauna

Grazing and reiteration of an oak root observed by in situ imaging.

title: Observing soil organisms in situ?
text:
From images to data
High-frequency automated monitoring generates a volume of data that quickly makes manual expertise incompatible with the available human and time resources. Generalizing imaging approaches, and more broadly moving towards soil ecology at large scale, therefore requires automated analysis pipelines able to process large image streams while maintaining an inference quality comparable to that of a human expert. We work on the design of such pipelines.


 Roots

Root structures
To extract biological information on root structures, we use RootPainter, a deep-learning-based tool developed at the University of Copenhagen. It requires a training phase for the model.
Associated publication 

The RootPainter annotation interface.



 Invertebrates

Soil invertebrates
For invertebrates, we developed our own tool, based on two steps: animal detection, using heuristic methods that differentiate successive images, and classification, using a deep-learning model. A Shiny interface was developed to train the model.
Associated publication 

The Shiny interface used to annotate invertebrates and train the model.

title: Emma Belaud
text:
Emma Belaud
    Soil ecology researcher
    
       GitHub
       ResearchGate
       ORCID
    
  
  


I work on soil ecology, with a focus on developing sensor-based monitoring methods. I recently completed my PhD, entitled “Soil ecology in the digital age: challenges and contributions of automated edaphic biodiversity monitoring.”. Through this work, I contributed to the development of a new in-situ soil imaging method that non-invasively monitors the dynamics of roots and soil invertebrates. I have explored what this method can reveal about the spatio-temporal organization of soil activity across ecological, spatial, and temporal scales.

A window into the soil

title: Who lives beneath our feet?
section: What do they do down there?
text:
What do they do down there?
Each organism has a main role in the soil, which we call its function. Grouping taxa by function gives three functional groups: decomposers, predators and ecosystem engineers.

title: Who lives beneath our feet?
text:
Decomposers: the recyclers


Decomposers feed on dead plants, dead animals and their droppings, and transform this organic matter step by step. The final step is mineralisation: matter is broken down into simple molecules, the nutrients that plants can finally use to grow.


  
    
  
  A leaf being broken down, seen through the scanner.

title: Who lives beneath our feet?
text:
Predators: the regulators
Predators eat other living organisms. When they eat crop pests, they directly benefit agriculture and are called beneficial organisms. More broadly, by keeping prey populations in check they let many species live side by side, which supports biodiversity.

title: Who lives beneath our feet?
text:
Engineers: the builders
Ecosystem engineers are large organisms that shape the structure of the soil as they move. Searching for food or shelter, they open up new spaces and dig networks of galleries. A well-structured soil has its mineral and organic particles assembled into aggregates of different sizes, leaving empty spaces between them: this is porosity.
This physical rearrangement of the soil by living organisms is called bioturbation. Earthworms are famous for it, but ants play their part too. The porosity they create lets water and air circulate and helps roots push through.

    Ants digging galleries.

title: Who lives beneath our feet?
text:
Fungi: underground highways


Fungi spread through the soil in search of food with a web of fine filaments called hyphae. This mycelium forms a vast network that carries nutrients over long distances.


  
    
  
  Fungal hyphae colonising the soil.



Fungi and roots: a deal that pays both ways
Fungi can associate with roots in a partnership called mycorrhization. The plant gives the fungus carbon-rich resources from photosynthesis. In return, the fungus supplies nutrients and water, acting as an extension of the root system. Fungi can explore about ten times more soil volume than roots alone, so the plant grows better, withstands harsh conditions better, and is better protected against outside threats.

  
    
      
    
    Ectomycorrhizae (ECM) on a root.
  
  
    
      
    
    Mycorrhization of a fine, branched root.

title: Who lives beneath our feet?
text:
Ants and their aphid herds
Roots are also a food source for soil herbivores such as aphids. Aphids have struck up a mutualistic deal with ants: the ants protect the aphids, which are prey for many predators, and in exchange feed on the sugary honeydew the aphids produce. When the pressure from these organisms gets too strong, this partnership can become a threat to crops.


  
    
  
  Ants tending aphids on a root.


  Aphids
  FormicidaeSolenopsis ants

title: Who lives beneath our feet?
text:
When grazing helps roots grow
Root grazing by soil fauna is not necessarily bad news for crops. If attacks stop the main root from growing, lateral roots emerge instead. This increases the contact surface between soil and roots, so nutrients are absorbed better. These finer, slower-growing lateral roots are also the ones fungi prefer to colonise.

  
    
  
  Soil fauna feeding on a root, and the root's response.

title: Who lives beneath our feet, and what do they do?
text:
Soil hosts almost a quarter of all the species described on Earth (Anthony et al., 2023).  This largely hidden life keeps ecosystems running and supports services we all depend on, from food production to carbon storage. To make the most of these services, we need to understand the biological processes behind them.
Yet we still know surprisingly little about how soil life works. Soil has been called one of the last biotic frontiers, along with the deep ocean and the forest canopy (André et al., 1994). The reason is simple: soil is opaque, and its inhabitants are small and hard to reach. Imaging gets around this problem.  The animations on this page come from images taken by flatbed scanners buried in the ground, which let us watch soil life where it happens, without digging it up.

title: Who lives beneath our feet, and what do they do?
text:
Fungi: underground highways


Fungi are found everywhere in the soil. They colonise it in search of food by growing a network of thread-like filaments called hyphae. This network works as an extensive transport system, carrying nutrients over long distances.


  
    
  
  Fungal hyphae colonising the soil.© Emma Belaud · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0



Fungi and roots: a deal that pays both ways
Some of these fungi form a partnership with plant roots, called mycorrhiza. It is a symbiosis, meaning both sides benefit: the plant gives the fungus carbon-rich compounds, and in return the fungus supplies the plant with nutrients and water, effectively extending its root system. Fungal hyphae can explore a volume of soil about 10 times larger than roots alone. As a result, mycorrhizal plants tend to grow better, cope better with harsh conditions and be better protected against external threats.

  
    
  
  Ectomycorrhizae (ECM) on a root.© Emma Belaud · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

Roots can also be attacked by soil animals. Root-feeding aphids, for example, use roots as their food source. They have developed a mutualistic relationship with ants: the ants protect the aphids from their many predators and, in return, feed on the sugary honeydew the aphids produce. When these populations become too dense, this partnership can threaten crops.

title: Who lives beneath our feet, and what do they do?
text:
When grazing helps roots grow
Root grazing by soil animals is not always bad news for crops. When herbivores halt the growth of the main root, the plant can respond by producing lateral roots. This increases the contact area between roots and soil, and therefore the plant’s ability to absorb nutrients. These finer, slower-growing roots are also the ones most readily colonised by mycorrhizal fungi, which brings us back to the partnership described above.

  
    
  
  Mycorrhization of a fine, branched root.© Emma Belaud · CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

title: Who lives beneath our feet, and what do they do?
text:
Decomposers


Decomposers feed on dead plants, dead animals and their droppings, and transform this organic matter step by step: they are the recyclers of the soil. Soil animals shred and mix the debris, and microorganisms then complete the job through mineralisation, which breaks matter down into simple molecules. These are the nutrients that plants can finally use to grow.

title: Who lives beneath our feet, and what do they do?
text:
Predators
Predators eat other living organisms, which makes them key players in biological regulation. By feeding on crop pests, they directly benefit agriculture and are called beneficial organisms. More broadly, by keeping prey populations in check, they can help many species live side by side (coexistence), which supports biodiversity. Not every member of these groups hunts, however: some mites, for example, feed on fungi or dead matter.

title: Who lives beneath our feet, and what do they do?
text:
Engineers
Ecosystem engineers shape the structure of the soil. As they move about in search of food or shelter, they dig and push material around, creating new spaces that change the habitat of all the other organisms. The animation shows ants starting to dig a network of tunnels. Earthworms and ants are the best-known engineers, but in reality every soil organism, even the smallest, contributes to mixing the soil and refining its structure.
A well-structured soil is made of mineral and organic particles assembled into aggregates of various sizes, with empty spaces in between (the porosity). These spaces let roots penetrate and let water and oxygen circulate.

text:
Zoom on bioturbation
The physical rearrangement of soil by living organisms has a name: bioturbation. Earthworms are widely known for it. Their burrowing creates pores that let water and air circulate and roots penetrate, as the animation shows.

title: Who lives beneath our feet, and what do they do?
section: How do we see all this?
text:
How do we see all this?
Everything you have just seen comes from images of the soil taken in situ by flatbed scanners buried underground, which photograph the same patch of soil again and again over time. To find out how the system works, see Soil biodiversity imaging.
